The analysis presented in Table 1 also depicted that the PLHIV who remained alive during the study period or who died in between, significantly differed from each other in terms of their socio-demographic, clinical and programme exposure related characteristics. For instance, the higher proportion of PLHIV those remained alive were female, literate, belonging to urban areas, were on ART, and had CD4 count above 350. Moreover, a larger proportion of surviving PLHIV had a longer duration of programme exposure. On the contrary, the proportion of PLHIV, who died during the interim intervention period, majority of them were aged 18 and above, ever married, were involved in income generation activities, did not undergo counting of CD4 and suffered from TB. A significantly higher proportion of PLHIV who died had less than six months of programme exposure.

### Estimation of mortality rates

Fig 1 shows the mortality rates among PLHIV by their characteristics. While the overall death rate was 38 deaths per 1000 persons per year, PLHIV, who were male, aged 18 and above, illiterate, and belonging to rural areas had higher mortality rates compared to their respective counterparts. On the other hand, higher chances of survival were noticed among those on ART and those without co-morbidity such as TB, compared to their respective counterparts.

### Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities

The study attempted to analyse the expected survival probability of PLHIV post they detected positive by selected characteristics such as sex, ART and CD4 status, and their duration of programme exposure. Considering the variations in accessibility to HIV care services by their place of residence (i.e., rural and urban), the survival probabilities were adjusted for their location of usual stay. Fig 2 shows the ten-year adusted survival probability curves among PLHIV since they tested positive for HIV. At the overall level, 738 PLHIV per 1000 person years expected to survive post ten years since they tested positive. The adjusted survival rates were higher among females (803 per 1000 person years) compared to males (669 per 1000 person-years) (Fig 3). Figs 4 and 5 show the ten-year adjusted survival probability curves for PLHIV by ART and CD4 status, respectively. As expected, those who were on ART had a higher likelihood of survival (788 per 1000) compared to those not on ART (690 per 1000) post ten years since tested HIV-positive. Similarly, increase in CD4 count from less than 100 to 249 increased the survival rate from 377 to 709 per 1000 person years, post ten years since tested HIV-positive. A further increase in CD4 count increased the survival rate to 885 per 1000 for the PLHIV having CD4 count 350 and above.

Fig 6 presents the adjusted survival probability curves for the duration of programme exposure for PLHIV post ten year period since they tested HIV-positive. As expected, there has been a significant increase in the survival rates with a gradual rise in the duration of programme exposure. For instance, the ten-year survival rates post detection to HIV increased from 391 per 1000 to 900 per 1000 person-years among those who had at 2 or more years of programme exposure compared to the PLHIV with less than six months of programme exposure, respectively.

The effect of programme exposure, ART treatment, and CD4 counts may be confounded by the background characteristics of PLHIV, and hence, survival probabilities can be tentative until they are adjusted for the effects of background factors. Table 2 presents the results of Cox Proportional Hazard Model estimating the risk of mortality by the associated risk factors. The analysis confirmed the already described findings that duration of programme exposure, being on ART, and higher CD4 counts reduced the mortality risks among PLHIV even after adjusting for potential confounding effects of the selected factors considered in the study. For instance, the mortality risk among PLHIV increases significantly with the increase in age (HR: 1.461; CI: 1.241–1.721) and due to presence of TB as co-infection (HR: 1.796; CI: 1.674–1.926) but decreases among females (HR: 0.679; CI: 0.636–0.725), those literate (HR: 0.690; CI: 0.650–0.733), working (HR: 0.848; CI: 0.791–0.908), and belong to the urban areas (HR: 0.706; CI: 0.662–0.753). Furthermore, being on ART and increase in CD4 count from less than 100 to 100–249 significantly reduces the mortality risk among PLHIV (HR: 0.627; CI: 0.585–0.673 & HR: 0.618; CI: 0.566–0.676, respectively). A further increase in CD4 count from 250 to 349 and from 350 and above reduces the death rate significantly. All these relationships were found to be statistically significant at 1 percent level of significance.

The most important result to notice from Table 2 is that PLHIV having at least one year of exposure to the intervention (1–2 years) had significantly lower risk of mortality (HR: 0.254; CI: 0.232–0.279); which subsequently reduced to 0.062 (CI 0.054–0.071) among those who had more than two years of intervention exposure while comparing with the PLHIV exposed to the intervention for just 6 months.

## Discussion

Based on the data derived from a retrospective cohort of patients living with HIV and registered with an intensive HIV care and support programme for PLHIV in selected districts of Karnataka, this study made an attempt to estimate the mortality rate and the probability of survival post ten-year intervention period among them. Only a few studies in India, till date, have made any effort to determine the mortality risk using the programme-based individual tracking data using a large sample size. Findings of this study documented the death rate of 38 per 1000 person-years, which was little higher than the death rates reported in the other parts of the country.[10, 12]

The study reported relatively higher mortality rates among males compared to females. This finding is somewhat contrary to the general belief that men have better access and utilization of health care services including HIV-testing and counseling, thereby, should have lower chances of mortality. However, because the intervention was primarily focussed on rural areas, the social stigma attached around HIV/AIDS may lead to the lower access of services among men. The role of stigma in limiting the access of services may not be so strong among females as the intervention had several focused activities to bring the females to the clinic periodically and serve them various health services that they need.[8] Existing studies have well documented the prevailing high levels of stigma associated with the HIV, at the community as well as the family level, in the similar type of rural context.[15] A higher number of male deaths as compared to females have been noticed in other studies also.[10, 12, 16–18] Such deaths are mostly contributed to a higher rate of loss to follow-up or delay in the initiation of ART at the most advanced stage of AIDS among males compared to females.[10] Programmatically, no doubt it is important to make females aware of the symptoms of HIV, places where HIV testing facility is available, as well as early detection of the infection, but more importantly males should also be intensively covered with the intervention so that they may enroll themselves in the care and support programme if detected positive. The higher deaths among males have also attributed to the biological differences in the drug response to ART among males and females.[10, 18]

Both bivariate and multivariate analysis showed a strong association between higher mortality rates and demographic variables such as age, educational level, and place of residence. The higher death rate among older ages has been found in other studies too.[10, 12, 19–25] Findings in these studies clearly indicated that the risk of mortality significantly increases with the increase in age while decreases with the increase in educational attainment.[12] The inadequate medical facility in the rural areas is found to be a contributing factor for the higher risk of mortality among HIV-patients in rural areas.[20–22, 24]

In agreement with the previous studies, the findings of this study also suggest lower death rate and a higher likelihood of survival among the PLHIV, who were on ART. Globally, in the absence of a cure for HIV, the increased use of ART has been able to improve the survival of individuals infected with HIV[26–28] by postponing their progression to death.[29, 30] The introduction of ART resulted in significant decline in the AIDS-related deaths not only in developed countries but also in India.[31–35] According to NACO, as a result of the extensive availability of ART therapy and increased uptake of these services has led to fewer AIDS-related deaths in India during 2011 than a decade ago.[2, 31] As a part of the initial assessment on the effectiveness of ART programme in India, a study from southern India reported a decline in the death rate from 25 deaths per 100 person years to 5 deaths among young PLHIV soon after initiation of ART.[36]

One of the significant finding of our study is that the likelihood of survival increases with the high level of CD4 count and it corraborates with the previous studies conducted in India.[37, 38] The chances of survival found in these studies were comparatively lower among the HIV-positive patients having lower CD4 count. Findings of our study clearly demonstrated the cascade of mortality among the PLHIV with the declining CD4 count. The minimum likelihood of death was observed among the PLHIV having CD4 count 350 and above whereas it was highest among those having the CD4 count less than 100. Previous studies have also found a relationship between low CD4 count and presence of opportunistic infection. For instance, PLHIV having CD4 count less than 200 at the time of HIV diagnosis had higher chances of acquiring other opportunistic infections such as TB.[31] Findings of our study also suggested the increased risk of mortality among the PLHIV diagnosed with other co-morbidities such as TB. Tuberculosis has appeared as one of the leading causes of deaths among patients infected with HIV.[31, 32] A higher proportion of deaths observed among HIV-positive individuals suffering from multiple infections, especially TB.[39, 40] Studies in India have clearly documented that PLHIV acquired selected opportunistic infections such as TB, oral candidiasis, and few other non-communicable diseases were at much higher risk of mortality compared to their counterparts having no such infections.[41–44]

Analysis conducted in this paper also focused on analyzing the effect of exposure to care and support intervention on the survival of PLHIV. It is clear that the survival probabilities improved as the duration of programme exposure increased. However, if the programme exposure is more than two years, there is hardly any further decrease in the survival probability post ten years since tested positive. Such relationship, of course, expected to depend upon CD4 count and whether the person is on ART or not. But results of the hazard model indicate that even after controlling for CD4 count and being on ART along with other background characteristics, the programme exposure alone reduces the risk of mortality drastically compared to who did not have any intervention exposure. The intervention exposure should have helped PLHIV to undergo the CD4 count test regularly and to get on ART treatment whenever necessary. However, intensive programme exposure for two years appears to be sufficient to sustain this behaviour.

Despite, the study observed various important findings including the minimum duration of intervention exposure required to reduce the mortality risk among PLHIV, the findings should be considered with caution. As the study was taken up using the retrospective data, some of the potential confounders of mortality such as viral load, previous histories of ART uptake, sequencing of co-infection, and side effects during the ART regime under the process of medication could not be included. The information on opportunistic infections, other than TB, was not properly captured. Similarly, the information on distance to ART center was not available. Therefore, our analysis could not use any information pertaining to the previous history of ART uptake presence of other opportunistic infections. Our results on the death rate might be overestimated due to the fact that all causes of death were included in the study and it is possible that certain deaths might have occurred due to non-HIV related causes. Due to a very large sample size, most of the bi-variate and multivarite results are statistically significant at one percent level of significance, and therefore, results should again be considered with caution. However, despite these limitations, many of the findings of this paper have importance from the planning of care and support programme and its implementation.

## Conclusions

The study revealed several useful results that have potential bearing on reducing the risk of mortality among the HIV-infected population. The most useful findings emerged from our analysis are adjusted hazard risks for CD4 status and duration of programme exposure. The increase in CD4 count from less than 100 to more than 350 reduced the hazard risk by more than 90 percent. An important question that was not properly answered till date was the required level of the CD4 count to reduce the hazard risk to zero. In fact, the even more relevant question to be asked is: what is an optimum level of the CD4 count for ART treatment? Our findings clearly demonstrated that a minimum CD4 count of 100 is required for the survival, whereas, CD4 count of more than 350 enhances the survival chances of PLHIV by multiple times. To maintain a high level of CD4 cell count among PLHIV, it is essential for the national programme to focus on the adherence of HIV-infected persons to ART therapy. Though the efforts are being made to improve the ART adherence among HIV-infected people and provision of free ART medicines at designated government ART centres have already been made under the national programme, still regular follow-up with the HIV-positive patients is required for better results. Further research is required to understand the reasons for non-adherence. Addressing the adherence in the ongoing ART programme in India may bring a notable reduction in the current level of mortality among HIV-infected persons.

Another significant finding of our paper is that the programme exposure of at least two years can brings a substantial reduction in the likelihood of mortality among PLHIV. More specifically, a focused care and support intervention with repeated follow-up and strategic use of information for ongoing improvement in the health and well-being of PLHIV has been critical in reducing the mortality. The project like Samastha that focused on medical and psycho-social services, regular follow-up of CD4 counts, and ART adherence contributed significantly to reduce mortality among PLHIV. For policy makers and programme implementers, it is definitely encouraging to know that exposure to a well-designed programme can become a good proxy for monitoring of CD4 counts and ART adherence.

# Heterogeneity of the HIV epidemic in the general population of Karnataka state, south India

## Abstract

Background: In the context of AVAHAN, the India AIDS Initiative of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, general population surveys (GPS) were carried out between 2006 and 2008 in Belgaum (northern), Bellary (mid-state) and Mysore (southern) districts of Karnataka state, south India. Data from these three surveys were analysed to understand heterogeneity in HIV risk.

Methods: Outcome variables were the prevalence of HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Independent variables included age, district, place of residence, along with socio-demographic, medical and behavioural characteristics. Multivariate logistic regression was undertaken to identify characteristics associated with HIV and differences between districts, incorporating survey statistics to consider weights and cluster effects.

Results: The participation rate was 79.0% for the interview and 72.5% for providing a blood or urine sample that was tested for HIV. Belgaum had the highest overall HIV (1.43%) and Herpes simplex type-2 (HSV-2) (16.93%) prevalence, and the lowest prevalence of curable STIs. In Belgaum, the HIV epidemic is predominantly rural, and among women. In Bellary, the epidemic is predominantly in urban areas and among men, and HIV prevalence was 1.18%. Mysore had the lowest prevalence of HIV (0.80%) and HSV-2 (10.89%) and the highest prevalence of curable STIs. Higher HIV prevalence among men was associated with increasing age (p<0.001), and with history of STIs (AOR=2.44,95%CI:1.15-5.17). Male circumcision was associated with lower HIV prevalence (AOR=0.33,95%CI:0.13-0.81). Higher HIV prevalence among women was associated with age (AOR25-29years=11.22,95%CI:1.42-88.74, AOR30-34years=13.13,95%CI:1.67-103.19 and AOR35-39years=11.33,95%CI:1.32-96.83), having more than one lifetime sexual partner (AOR=4.61,95%CI:1.26-16.91) and having ever used a condom (AOR=3.32,95%CI:1.38-7.99). Having a dissolved marriage (being widowed/divorced/separated) was the strongest predictor (AOR=10.98,95%CI: 5.35-22.57) of HIV among women. Being a muslim woman was associated with lower HIV prevalence (AOR=0.27,95%CI:0.08-0.87).

Conclusion: The HIV epidemic in Karnataka shows considerable heterogeneity, and there appears to be an increasing gradient in HIV prevalence from south to north. The sex work structure in the northern districts may explain the higher prevalence of HIV in northern Karnataka. The higher prevalence of HIV and HSV-2 and lower prevalence of curable STIs in Belgaum suggests a later epidemic phase. Similarly, higher prevalence of curable STIs and lower HIV and HSV-2 prevalence in Mysore suggests an early phase epidemic.

title: Progress and challenges towards eliminating vertical transmission of HIV in India - Scientific Reports
content:
Download PDF

## Abstract

India has intensified efforts towards elimination of vertical transmission of HIV (EVTH) as part of National AIDS and STD Control Programme-V (NACP-V). We present the progress in achieving NACP-V’s EVTH goal as of year 2023-24. We analysed the 2023 state level data using Spectrum model in 2023 to measure the coverage of anti-retroviral treatment among pregnant women, annual paediatric HIV case incidence rate and final vertical transmission rate. UNAIDS and WHO definitions for these indicators were used. In 2023, around 2350 new paediatric infections were estimated by vertical transmission. However, 44% of these transmissions resulted from incident HIV infections among pregnant and breastfeeding women. Overall, paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births decreased from 25.2 (14.7–46.6) in 2019 to 10.4 (6.1–19.3) in 2023. During the same reference period, final vertical transmission rate (inclusive of breastfeeding period) decreased from 25.28% (17.06–37.99) in 2019 to 11.75% (7.93–17.66) in 2023. The 2023 India HIV estimates, using recent data and global modelling tools, highlighted progress in eliminating vertical transmission of HIV. Early identification of HIV-positive mothers and starting them on lifelong ART is crucial. Additionally, generating local evidence is needed on interventions like safe practices, repeat testing, and feeding practices to inform policy decisions.

## Introduction

In the early 2000 s, evidence demonstrated that administering antiretroviral (ARV) medications to women living with HIV during their pregnancy and breastfeeding can reduce the vertical HIV transmission rates to under 5%1,2,3,4. As a result, UNAIDS and WHO identified elimination of vertical transmission of HIV (EVTH) as a public health priority in 20095,6. Since then, substantial global guidelines for concerted actions have emerged with specific indicators to measure the attainment of EVTH7,8,9,10. This encompassed achieving impact indicators, including an annual paediatric HIV incidence of less than 50 per 100,000 live births and a final vertical (both perinatal and postnatal) HIV transmission rate under 5% in breastfeeding population (or < 2% in non-breastfeeding populations). In 2023, global ARV coverage rate among 1.20 million (0.95–1.40 million) HIV positive pregnant women was 84% (72->95%) with final vertical transmission rate of 10% (8–13%)11. Till September 2024, 18 countries have received World Health Organization (WHO) validation certificate for EVTH12.

Use of models like Spectrum is an accepted approach to assess progress on vertical transmission indicators10,11. Spectrum, developed by Avenir Health (www.avenirhealth.org) in collaboration with UN agencies like WHO and UNAIDS, is a user-friendly suite of policy models that equips user with a robust analytical tool to inform decision-making and support evidence-based planning. The tool is used for estimating the demographic ramifications of the HIV/AIDS pandemic, encompasses the AIDS Impact Model (AIM) module, which simulates the complex interplay between demographic, epidemiological, and programmatic factors influencing the trajectory of the HIV epidemic. By integrating a myriad of data inputs, including antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage, mother-to-child transmission probabilities, and mortality rates, AIM generates a nuanced and multifaceted portrait of the epidemic’s impact on population dynamics, including that of vertical transmission rates, thereby informing the development of evidence-based policy interventions, resource allocation strategies, and service delivery modalities.

India, with around 2.54 million people living with HIV (PLHIV), is home to the second largest number of PLHIV across the globe11. Government of India is implementing the National AIDS and STD Control Programme (NACP) since 1992 driven by evidence-led, evolving, and comprehensive response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic13. Specific interventions for prevention of parents to child transmission (PPTCT) under NACP were initiated during phase-2 (1999–2007) of the programme. Single dose Nevirapine (sdNVP) was the cornerstone of the PPTCT programme under NACP till 2011 (NACP-3). In 2012, when NACP-IV was initiated, triple-drug ARV regimens throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding (Option B) were introduced. The strategy was further modified in 2013 with a policy of initiation and life-long retention on triple ARVs as soon as pregnant women were diagnosed with HIV infection14. The initial goal was to achieve the elimination of vertical HIV transmission by 2015, but this target year was later moved to 2020. NACP adopted dual elimination of vertical transmission of HIV and syphilis as a priority area in its strategic plan for the period of 2017-2415.

In 2020-21, around 23 million HIV tests were done among pregnant women in India against an estimated 30 million pregnant women in the country. In the same year, against the estimated size of nearly 21,000 HIV positive pregnant women requiring services for prevention of vertical transmission of HIV, around 11,000 were put on life-long ARVs and an overall vertical transmission rate of more than 20% was estimated16,17.

NACP phase V, launched to anchor the national AIDS and STD response for the five-year period of 2021-22 to 2025-26, focused on elimination of vertical transmission of HIV as one of the five high-level goals to fast-track the progress. By increasing coverage of HIV testing among pregnant women and getting every HIV positive pregnant woman initiated and retained on ARVs in collaboration with the public health systems as well as the private sector, the goal focussed on attaining elimination of vertical transmission in alignment with WHO recommendations by 2025-2618. In this paper, we present the progress made towards attainment of this third goal of NACP-V until the year 2023-24, which is the third year of implementation of the NACP-V. The objective is to analyse the trends of impact indicators of paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births and final vertical HIV transmission rate as per WHO recommended targets for elimination using the State-wise Spectrum models for the 2023 round of estimates.

## Methods

Both HIV surveillance and HIV burden estimation are institutionalised annual activities under the NACP that provide up-to-date information on the magnitude and direction of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the country and its constituent states as well as union territories19,20. This activity is done by formally engaging government institutes and indicators pertaining to prevalence, incidence, mortality, and vertical transmission of HIV by State and Union Territory are annually estimated. The Spectrum mathematical model, developed by Avenir Health, UNAIDS, and partners, is utilised for this purpose.

### HIV burden Estimation using spectrum model

Globally, 170 countries use the Spectrum modelling tool to assess the impact of HIV on their populations. This tool is regularly updated to account for the latest scientific evidence on demographics, programme impact, fertility, mortality and incidence under guidance and direction of the UNAIDS Reference Group on Estimates, Modelling and Projections. The procedures and methodology are discussed in detail elsewhere21,22.

In essence, Spectrum models are based on demography, treatment coverage, and HIV prevalence data to generate HIV incidence estimates and trends by age, sex, and CD4 + counts. The dynamic nature of the model permits transitioning of newly infected individuals over time with change in age, CD4 + count, and treatment (or non-treatment) categories. Typically, the Spectrum output is estimation of the PLHIV population by age and sex every year. Adjusted fertility rates are applied to Women living with HIV (WLHIV) aged 15–49 to estimate HIV-positive mothers requiring ARV treatment to achieve elimination of vertical transmission. Adjusted fertility rates for WLHIV account for the influence of HIV infection on fertility23,24. The model subsequently estimates the vertical transmission rate by considering the type and coverage of ARV treatment alongside the probability of vertical transmission by type and duration of ARV coverage during the perinatal and breastfeeding phases25,26.

### HIV estimates 2023 under NACP of India

In India, disease burden is estimated annually using State/Union Territory (UT)-specific models, except for the union territory of Lakshadweep, which lacks surveillance data. The UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are modelled together since Ladakh currently does not have sufficient surveillance data to be independently assessed. For performing HIV Estimates 2023, Spectrum 6.33 version was employed.

Each model was set-up for the period of 1981 to 2036. The Spectrum modelling tool typically sets the start year five years prior to the first reported case of local HIV transmission. Consistent with this approach, the State/UT model in India initializes simulations in 1981, projecting forward to 2036. This extended timeframe enables policymakers to forecast the potential magnitude and trajectory of the epidemic beyond the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, facilitating proactive planning and strategic decision-making to address the evolving needs of the HIV response.

State models for the 2022 round of estimates were updated with the India and State-specific latest data on ARV coverage and HIV prevalence generated through routine programme monitoring, surveillance surveys and national family health survey data. Default parameters were retained only when India or State-specific evidence on that parameter was not available. All of the models were aggregated using the ‘Aggregate’ function of the Spectrum to produce the national estimates. HIV Estimates 2023 was done through a tiered institutional arrangement comprising working and review by Technical Subgroup (HIV Burden Estimation), Technical Working Group (Surveillance & Epidemiology) and Technical Resource Group (Surveillance & Epidemiology).

At the national level, the aggregated number of pregnant women receiving ARVs for eliminating vertical transmission was around 17,700; the highest in the country since the launch of the programme (Fig. 1).

Data on breastfeeding practices were also updated in 2023 round based on the programme data. ### Fertility adjustments and vertical transmission patterns update

In each State/UT-model, data on total fertility rate and age-specific fertility rate were inputted based on the Sample Registration System (Registrar General Government of India). The inputted fertility data were adjusted to account for the influence of HIV infection on fertility. The Default Spectrum values for age-specific fertility adjustments for HIV + women on and off ART were retained (Supplementary Table 1) in the absence of India-specific data on the same. The ‘Fit local adjustment factor’ button in Spectrum was used to best fit the fertility reduction value to data on prevalence among pregnant women. Spectrum had provisioned this feature to improve the match to prevalence among pregnant women and the estimated PMTCT coverage. The probability of vertical transmission of HIV depends on the stage of infection of the mother, the duration of breastfeeding and the ARV regimen. The default rates in Spectrum were not changed (Supplementary Table 2).

### Prevalence data updates

Epidemic configuration for each State/UT model was set-up as concentrated epidemic. Under this pattern, 15–49 yrs population in each State/UT model was distributed among five populations subgroups viz. female sex workers (FSW), men who have sex with men (MSM), hijra/transgender (H/TG) persons, people who inject drugs (PWID), and general population.

For the population subgroups of FSW, MSM, H/TG and PWID, the prevalence data was updated till the year 2023 based on the HIV prevalence data from sentinel surveillance and positivity data among these populations from routine testing under the programme. For the general population, the epidemic data was updated till 2023 using the HIV sentinel surveillance data and routine testing data among pregnant women. Data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-3 and NFHS-4) were also inputted to inform the HIV epidemic curve in the general population.

### Epidemic curve fitting and calibration

‘Spectrum’ offers various modelling options, including *Estimation and Projection Package (EPP) Classic* and *R-Hybrid*, for generating epidemic curves. The recommendation is to use *EPP Classic* in scenarios where prevalence data is limited while to use *R-Hybrid* when multiple years of prevalence data from multiple sites are available. HIV burden estimations under NACP use the *EPP Classic* and *R-Hybrid* models.

EPP Classic uses four parameters: time of epidemic start (t-zero), the proportion of the susceptible population at risk of HIV infection (f-zero) at t-zero, transmission rate for untreated adults (r), and behavior change rate.

R-Hybrid combines two different models of the transmission rate: one for the initial stages of the epidemic and another for more recent trends. Until the 2000 s, the R-hybrid model utilized a four-parameter logistic function to represent the transmission rate: log of the initial epidemic growth rate, log endemic transmission rate after the epidemic has stabilized, rate of decline of the log transmission rate as the epidemic stabilizes, and time of the inflection point of the logistic function. From the mid-2000s, when HIV epidemics are considered to have stabilized to a state of endemic transmission dynamics, the model used a piecewise-linear spline with a first-order random-walk (RW1) penalty on the spline coefficients to model changes in log r(t). The piecewise-linear spline allows the transmission rate to vary with recent epidemic trends, whereas the RW1 penalty assumes that the expected transmission rate remains steady with linearly increasing variance.

For the general population, R-Hybrid model was used to do the epidemic curve fittings for all States with at least 10 surveillance sites among pregnant women. Among the rest, EPP classic model was used to do epidemic curve fittings for the general population. For rest of the population groups, EPP classic curve fittings was used. During curve fittings, prevalence conditions were applied to remove the unrealistic curves in line with UNAIDS recommendations27. The Spectrum modelling process advises applying prevalence conditions to exclude unrealistic scenarios when default randomly generated curves contradict expert opinion or epidemiological evidence. For example, if curves depict implausibly rapid and high epidemics inconsistent with a country’s epidemiological record, a constraint such as ‘prevalence in 1985 must be less than 5%’ can be applied. Following this approach, state/UT-specific prevalence conditions in 2023 round were applied based on local knowledge and evidence.

HIV burden estimate process in India calibrates the epidemic curve generated through EPP Classic/R-hybrid using the data from probability-based survey in community settings to account for inherent biases in facility-based surveillance28,30. The curve fitting and calibration method used in the Spectrum modelling tool is detailed elsewhere31,35. EPP is calibrated using a Bayesian approach namely Incremental Mixture Importance Sampling (IMIS). IMIS identifies points with high importance weights in areas where the target density is underrepresented. Each iteration adds a multivariate normal distribution centered at the highest weight point to the importance sampling distribution, forming a mixture with the prior. This process iteratively improves representation of underrepresented parameter space, creating an importance sampling distribution that accurately covers the target distribution. Further, the model calculates a calibration constant to account for the difference between the surveillance-fitted prevalence and the observed prevalence from population survey. This constant is applied to each prevalence trajectory, and then re-sampling of scaled trajectories is done to generated adjust epidemic curves in alignment with representative surveys prevalence. This approach allows for the incorporation of population survey data into the model, enabling more accurate estimates of HIV prevalence.

In 2023 round, the calibration on general population was not applied for 4 states, viz., Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura, Punjab, and Rajasthan. This was done because applying calibration was leading to a PLHIV size estimates which was lower than the actual number of PLHIV currently under the programme. In the next step, the sex ratios and incidence rate ratios were updated according to the epidemic type (Concentrated non-IDU or Concentrated IDU pattern) within Spectrum’s ‘sex/age pattern’ Table36.

### Uncertainty analysis and aggregation

Uncertainty analysis represents the concluding phase in updating a State model. This was accomplished using the ‘Uncertainty analysis’ tool within Spectrum. The tool produces plausible range of estimates for critical epidemiological outputs by conducting 1000 Monte Carlo iterations. These iterations take into considerations uncertainties in adult incidence along with uncertainties around other essential assumptions such as fertility, incidence, and mortality, based on global or regional data. Spectrum’s default values for mean and standard deviation on uncertainty variables were applied in absence of India-specific data. The national estimates were generated by aggregating the State model using the “Aggregate” tool of Spectrum.

### Description of indicators used in results

We present the analysis of outputs generated through the HIV Estimations 2023 model at State and national level on the indicators of EVTH-service coverage, paediatric HIV incidence rate and vertical HIV transmission rate. The descriptions of the presented indicators are given below36.

1. a.

   HIV-positive mothers in need of ARVs for prevention of vertical transmission: The number of HIV-positive women giving birth each year and, therefore, in need of ARVs to prevent HIV transmission to the baby.
2. b.

   % HIV-positive mothers initiated on ARV: The percentage of HIV-positive mothers needing ARVs who are receiving it in that year.
3. c.

   New paediatric infections due to vertical transmission: The number of children who become infected due to vertical transmission in a year. This includes perinatal transmission and up to 36 months of breastfeeding.
4. d.

   Vertical transmission rate at 6 weeks: The percentage of babies born to HIV + mothers who are infected by 6 weeks of age.
5. e.

   Final vertical transmission rate including breastfeeding period (%): The percentage of children born to HIV + mothers who will eventually be infected due to vertical transmission at current transmission rates. This includes perinatal transmission and up to 36 months of breastfeeding.
6. f.

   Vertical transmission by source: Disaggregation of new vertical infections by timing (prenatal or during breastfeeding) and ARV (on an off) regimen.

### Ethics statement

HIV surveillance and estimation was an ongoing activity under NACP done through a robust institutional arrangement. Prior to each round, the institutes presented their methodology and ethical considerations to their ethics committees for approval. Data collection under the surveillance survey was undertaken upon receiving local ethics committee approval. Institute ethics committee of All India Institute of Medical Sciences (India, New Delhi) approved the ethical considerations for the 2023 round of HSS vide reference no IEC-629/15.07.2022 dated 15.07.2022. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant operational guidelines and ethical considerations approved by the Ethical Committee. Data collection in surveillance was done as per the approved method after obtained written informed consents from selected respondents. HIV burden estimation was carried out through the institutional arrangements by utilising aggregated, de-identified data following each round of HIV surveillance.

## Results

Nationally, 19,962 (16,403 − 24,737) HIV-positive mothers were in need of ARVs for prevention of vertical transmission (Table 2). Overall coverage for ARVs in HIV-positive mothers in 2023 was 89.02% (71.96 - >=95) with a vertical transmission rate of 5.06% (2.98–8.47) at 6 weeks and final transmission rate (including breastfeeding period) of 11.75% (7.93–17.66). Overall, 2339 (1372–4344) new vertical HIV infections were estimated among children of which around 44% were from women who acquired incident HIV infections either during pregnancy (8%) or breastfeeding (36%) (Fig. 3). Another 22% were from women who did not receive ARVs during pregnancy. 12% of estimated vertical transmission were among HIV-positive mothers who didn’t receive ARV during breastfeeding; 8% were among HIV-positive mothers who dropped off from ARV during pregnancy; while another 5% were among mothers who dropped off from ARV during breastfeeding.

## Discussion

Eliminating vertical transmission of HIV is central to India’s commitment of ending AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. The NACP-V (2021-22 to 2025-26) aims for, *inter alia*, an annual paediatric HIV incidence below 50 per 100,000 live births and a vertical HIV transmission rate under 5% by 2025-2618. We measured State/UT-wise progress on these impact indicators up to 2023-24. Although an enormous progress has been observed nationally, a very diverse and complex scenario unfolded sub-nationally thereby underlining the need for tailored strategies.

As NACP-V intensifies focus on elimination of vertical HIV transmission by adopting it as one of the five top level goals, there is a dramatic progress on related impact indicators. Paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births decreased from 25.2 in 2019 to 10.4 in 2023 while final vertical transmission rate (including breastfeeding period) decreased from 25.28% in 2019 to 11.75% in 2023. Progress on impact indicators targets had been accompanied by significant increase in ARV coverage among WLHIV for EVTH which increased from 60.42% in 2019 to 89.02% in 2023. This had been most evident in the States of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh where the final vertical transmission was very near to the target level of 5%. In these States ARV coverage among HIV positive mothers was more than 90%.

Overall, around 2350 new paediatric vertical infections were estimated to happen in 2023; almost 59% lower than the estimate for 2019. A significant proportion (44%) of these vertical transmissions resulted from women with incident HIV infections, either during pregnancy or during breastfeeding period. In States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Punjab, and Tripura, at least 60% of the total vertical infections were from women who had incident HIV infections. These were States where overall HIV incidence rate was higher than the national average37.

Incident HIV among pregnant and breastfeeding women, coupled with the significant risk of vertical transmission, poses a well-documented challenge to achieving the elimination of vertical transmission of HIV38,39,40,41. Vertical transmission likelihood is as high as 18% among newly infected pregnant women. If the maternal HIV infection occurs during breastfeeding, the probability of vertical transmission can rise to 27%25,26. Couple counselling that encourages safe behaviours, greater involvement of male partners in adopting safe sexual practices during pregnancy and breastfeeding, including pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), have been recommended in various contexts to prevent new HIV infections among women42,43,44,45,46.

The WHO recommends repeat HIV testing to ensure early diagnosis of new HIV cases during pregnancy and breastfeeding47. This recommendation has been incorporated into the national HIV testing guidelines for EVTH-related services in many countries48. Studies in diverse settings, including in India, have demonstrated repeat HIV testing as a cost-effective strategy for EVTH49,50. Implementation research for testing the strategies for primary prevention for HIV infections among pregnant and breastfeeding women, as well as early identification of incident infections, at least in States/UTs where HIV incidence rate is high, will be critical for India’s progress on EVTH.

Around 21% of the total 2350 new paediatric vertical infections in 2023 in India occurred during breastfeeding period from mothers who had a HIV infection prior to the last delivery. HIV transmission through breastfeeding is well documented51,52,53,54. In Spectrum modelling tool (v6.33), based on experts’ review, transmission probabilities among non-incident HIV-positive breastfeeding women was set in the range of 0.51-0.89% per month for off-ART mothers and in the range of 0.02-0.20% per month for on-ART mothers depending upon CD4 count and duration of treatment25,26.

The probability of HIV transmission through breastfeeding poses a significant policy challenge. Breastfeeding is promoted globally, including in India, for its essential role in reducing infant mortality and under-five mortalities through optimal nutrition, protection against infections, and aiding in child spacing55,56,57,58. The risk of HIV transmission through breastfeeding versus the high morbidity and mortality-risk without it has led to evolving guidelines on feeding practices for exposed infants. This included endorsing decision of replacement feeding, in 2001, by mothers under proper counselling supporting settings where it is acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable, and safe (AFASS)51,52,53,,55,56,57,,59. WHO current guidelines recommend that country health authorities decide if HIV-infected mothers should either breastfeed with antiretrovirals or avoid breastfeeding60,61,62. In countries promoting breastfeeding, HIV-positive mothers should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue up to 24 months or longer while being on lifelong ART. The Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have recommended that women who are HIV-positive should not breastfeed to reduce perinatal HIV transmission in the United States63,64.

Impact of infant feedings choices vary by country context. Replacement feeding, together with lifelong ART have been positively associated with significant gains in prevention of vertical transmission, especially in high-income countries, and have been included in intervention packages by countries65,66,67,68,69. However, evidence has also indicated that the reductions in HIV transmission achieved through replacement feeding can be counterbalanced by increases in HIV-unrelated morbidities and mortalities, particularly in developing countries70,71,72,73. Economic and social contexts of replacement feeding have further compromised health outcomes for mothers and exposed babies59,74,75. Replacement feeding is linked to significantly reduced rates of vertical transmission. Nevertheless, it is essential to generate evidence specific to India to ascertain whether the advantages of replacement feeding outweigh the risks of non-HIV morbidity and mortality associated with the lack of breastfeeding for HIV-exposed infants.

Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have emerged as priority states to achieve elimination goals in the country. Uttar Pradesh had a population of approximately 233 million, while Bihar’s population is around 125 million76. These states also had the highest total fertility rates, at 3.0 in Bihar and 2.7 in Uttar Pradesh. Due to their large population size and high fertility rates, these two states accounted for nearly 20% of the total EVTH-service needs in the country. While the coverage of EVTH-services in Uttar Pradesh was about 92%, it stands at approximately 55% in Bihar, with the final vertical transmission rate reaching 29%. More than half of the vertical transmissions in Bihar were estimated to occur among children whose mothers did not receive ARV treatment during pregnancy or delivery. Uptake of antenatal care services in Bihar was low, only 68% of the mothers reported receipt of antenatal care for their last birth from a health professional while one-fifth reported not receiving any antenatal care services77. Sustained focus on augmenting family planning, antenatal care, HIV testing and ART initiation in collaboration with routine maternal, and child health services would be the key to making progress on vertical transmission in such States69,78. Repeat HIV tests in the third trimester, during labour, and/or while breastfeeding can significantly aid progress by identifying mothers who have recently contracted HIV, allowing them to join long-term HIV care and start ART42,43,44,45,46,47,48,49,50. Equally important will be focus on Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Sikkim, Tripura, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, and Puducherry as the final transmission rate in these States/UT in amongst the highest in the country. Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh have a rising HIV incidence which further underlines the need for urgent attention. Other States with rising HIV incidence (Punjab, Assam, and Meghalaya) will also augment their progress on EVTH with concerted efforts for interventions among pregnant and recently delivered women.

### Limitations

Estimating vertical transmission using the Spectrum modelling tool involves specific limitations, which have been previously mentioned in the context of HIV vertical transmission estimation in India21,26,79,80. The 2023 India HIV Estimates utilized State/UT-specific data on input parameters such as coverage, retention, and breastfeeding patterns for HIV-positive women covered in the programme. However, the data on fertility adjustments and vertical transmission probabilities employed default values provided within the model. Many of these defaults’ values are based on studies coming from foreign settings which may or may not be applicable for Indian context36. Conducting a nationally representative study to update the parameters pertaining to HIV impact on fertility and vertical transmission probabilities will be important for NACP.

Another limitation of this study is that the outputs of the Spectrum model were not validated against empirical data. Programme data from paediatric HIV diagnoses and ART initiations could be used to validate the model’s estimates of vertical transmission. A consistency across States in the ratio of number of paediatric HIV diagnoses to the modelled number of vertical transmissions would provide insights into modelled estimates. If that ratio isn’t stable, it could point to problems with the programme data, problems with the model assumptions, or both. Currently, this validation by using programme data cannot be undertaken for three primary reasons. Firstly, the detection of HIV-positive pregnant women under the programme against the estimated need is not uniform. Secondly, the testing of HIV-positive exposed infants at 6 weeks, 6 months and 18 months under the programme against the reported live-births vary significantly inter-State. Thirdly, data reported under the early infant diagnosis programme refers to the number of tests conducted, rather than the number of infants who received the tests, which hampers the correct understanding of vertical transmission rate from the programmatic data. Future efforts to strengthen the cohort-based longitudinal data reporting could enhance the feasibility of using available data sources to validate the model’s outputs and refine its assumptions.

Future progress monitoring on EVTH goal would benefit from conducting sensitivity analyses. Such analyses would allow for the exploration of how variations in model parameters, assumptions, and data sources impact the estimated outcomes. By undertaking sensitivity analyses, there can be better understanding of the potential sources of uncertainty and identify areas where further data collection or refinement of model parameters is warranted. This would ultimately enhance the reliability and generalizability of estimation results, providing policymakers and stakeholders with more accurate and informative evidence to guide decision-making.

The Spectrum modelling tool defines vertical transmission rate as the percentage of children born to HIV + mothers who will eventually be infected due to vertical transmission at current transmission rates. However, mothers who seroconvert during breastfeeding are not included in the denominator. Ideally, they should be. For India, the estimated vertical transmission rate is 11.75% (2339 transmissions out of 19,962). However, if we include the estimated 2911 mothers who seroconvert during breastfeeding in the denominator, the rate drops to 10.23% (2339 transmissions out of 22,873). Given the importance of accurate vertical transmission rates, it’s essential to include mothers who seroconvert during breastfeeding in the denominator.

## Conclusion

India HIV estimates 2023 utilized the latest version of globally recommended modelling tool and incorporated the most recent State/UT-specific data on demographics, programme coverage, and prevalence. The study highlighted significant progress made towards eliminating vertical transmission of HIV. However, there is no room for complacency. Traditional interventions, such as early identification of HIV-positive mothers and initiating them on life-long ART, remain essential to eliminating vertical transmission of HIV in India. Generating local evidence on the effectiveness of interventions, such as adoption of safe practices, repeat testing during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and feeding practices, will inform policy formulation for prevention and detection of incident infections. Future research exploring regional patterns and their correlates with socioeconomic factors will enable policy deliberations and actions improving healthcare outcomes.

title: Strengthening government management capacity to scale up HIV prevention programs through the use of Technical Support Units: lessons from Karnataka state, India
content:
## ABSTRACT

Scaling up HIV prevention programming among key populations (female sex workers and men who have sex with men) has been a central strategy of the Government of India. However, state governments have lacked the technical and managerial capacity to oversee and scale up interventions or to absorb donor-funded programs. In response, the national government contracted Technical Support Units (TSUs), teams with expertise from the private and nongovernmental sectors, to collaborate with and assist state governments. In 2008, a TSU was established in Karnataka, one of 6 Indian states with the highest HIV prevalence in the country and where monitoring showed that its prevention programs were reaching only 5% of key populations. The TSU provided support to the state in 5 key areas: assisting in strategic planning, rolling out a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation system, providing supportive supervision to intervention units, facilitating training, and assisting with information, education, and communication activities. This collaborative management model helped to increase capacity of the state, enabling it to take over funding and oversight of HIV prevention programs previously funded through donors. With the combined efforts of the TSU and the state government, the number of intervention units statewide increased from 40 to 126 between 2009 and 2013. Monthly contacts with female sex workers increased from 5% in 2008 to 88% in 2012, and with men who have sex with men, from 36% in 2009 to 81% in 2012. There were also increases in the proportion of both populations who visited HIV testing and counseling centers (from 3% to 47% among female sex workers and from 6% to 33% among men who have sex with men) and sexually transmitted infection clinics (from 4% to 75% among female sex workers and from 7% to 67% among men who have sex with men). Changes in sexual behaviors among key populations were also documented. For example, between 2008 and 2010, the proportion of surveyed female sex workers in 9 districts reporting that they used a condom at last intercourse rose from 60% to 68%; in 6 districts, the proportion of surveyed men who have sex with men reporting that they used a condom at last anal sex increased from 89% to 97%. The Karnataka experience suggests that TSUs can help governments enhance managerial and technical resources and leverage funds more effectively. With careful management of the working and reporting relationships between the TSU and the state government, this additional capacity can pave the way for the government to improve and scale up programs and to absorb previously donor-funded programs.
